concepts.name: Extracting facts accurately
concepts.description: Pull every number out of the paragraph, noting exactly what each one refers to.

concepts.name: Organizing scattered facts
concepts.description: Turn the paragraph into a short list or mini-table before calculating anything.

concepts.name: Stated vs derived values
concepts.description: Some numbers are given directly; others ("the remaining", "the rest") must be calculated first.

concepts.name: Translating relative statements
concepts.description: Phrases like "half of", "twice as many" or "20 more than" translate directly into simple equations.

concepts.name: Chaining facts together
concepts.description: Most caselet questions need two or more of the paragraph's facts combined, not just one.

formulas.title: Read once, then extract
formulas.prompt: What is the most reliable way to work through a caselet?
formulas.formula: Read the whole paragraph once for the story, then re-read it slowly, writing down every number and what it refers to
formulas.explanation: Trying to calculate while reading for the first time is the most common source of caselet mistakes — separate understanding from calculating.
formulas.example: Jot down "Total = 300", "Sales = 40% of total", "Marketing = half of Sales", etc. as you find them
formulas.commonMistake: Starting to calculate before every relevant fact has been located.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What should you do before performing any calculation in a caselet question?

formulas.title: Translating relative statements
formulas.prompt: How do you turn a phrase like "half the number in Sales" into a number you can use?
formulas.formula: Translate the phrase into an equation using the already-known quantity, then solve
formulas.explanation: Relative statements always refer back to a quantity stated earlier in the same paragraph — find that quantity first.
formulas.example: "Marketing is half of Sales" and Sales = 120 → Marketing = 120 ÷ 2 = 60
formulas.commonMistake: Applying the relative statement to the wrong base quantity.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If Sales has 120 employees and Marketing is half that number, how many are in Marketing?

formulas.title: Finding "the remaining"
formulas.prompt: How do you handle a phrase like "the remaining employees"?
formulas.formula: Remaining = Total − (sum of every group already accounted for)
formulas.explanation: Always subtract from the same total the other groups were defined against.
formulas.example: Total 300, with 120 in Sales and 60 in Marketing: remaining = 300 − 120 − 60 = 120
formulas.commonMistake: Subtracting from the wrong total, or forgetting to subtract one of the earlier groups.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Out of 300 total, 120 are in Sales and 60 are in Marketing. How many remain?

formulas.title: Turn the paragraph into a grid
formulas.prompt: A caselet has two ways of splitting the same people. How do you keep track?
formulas.formula:
Draw a 2 × 2 (or larger) grid with totals on the edges.
Fill what is given, then complete by subtraction.
formulas.explanation: Every row and column must add to its total, so each new number fixes others.
formulas.example: Of 120 staff, 70 are men; 40 men and 25 women are graduates. Non-graduate women = (120 − 70) − 25 = 25.
formulas.commonMistake: Answering from the paragraph directly and mixing up "of the men" with "of all staff".
formulas.applicationPrompt: Of 200 voters, 110 are women; 60% of the men and half the women voted. How many did not vote?

levels.title: Reading Before Calculating
levels.description: A caselet hides its data in prose — the skill is extracting it accurately before doing any arithmetic.

blocks.title: No chart, no table — just careful reading
blocks.body: A caselet describes numbers inside a paragraph instead of a chart or table. The math is usually simple once every fact is found; almost every mistake comes from misreading or missing a fact, not from the arithmetic.

blocks.title: Read, then extract
blocks.body: Read once for the story, then re-read while writing down every number and what it refers to
blocks.caption: Never start calculating during the first read-through.

blocks.body: "The remaining" always means the total minus everything already accounted for — check you have subtracted every earlier group.

levels.title: Caselet DI Formulas
levels.description: Organizing facts, translating relative statements, and finding "the remaining" amount.

levels.title: Direct Extraction
levels.description: Pulling out directly stated and simply derived facts.

levels.title: Chaining Multiple Facts
levels.description: Combining several facts to answer questions the paragraph doesn't state directly.

questions.question: How many employees work in Sales?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.method: Apply the stated percentage to the total.

hints.text: This is a directly stated percentage of the total.

commonMistakes: Using the wrong total to apply the percentage.

questions.question: How many employees work in Marketing?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.explanation: Marketing is half of Sales. Sales = 120, so Marketing = 120 ÷ 2 = 60.
questions.method: Find Sales first, then halve it.

hints.text: "Half of Sales" needs the Sales figure first.

commonMistakes: Halving the total (300) instead of Sales.

questions.question: How many employees work in Operations?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.explanation: Remaining = 300 − 120 (Sales) − 60 (Marketing) = 120, split equally between Operations and Finance: 120 ÷ 2 = 60 each.
questions.method: Find the remaining total first, then split it equally.

hints.text: "Remaining" means what is left after Sales and Marketing are removed.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract Marketing before finding the remainder.

questions.question: What is the monthly salary bill for the Sales department (in ₹ lakh)?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.explanation: Sales has 120 employees at ₹30,000 each: 120 × 30,000 = ₹36,00,000 = ₹36 lakh.
questions.method: Multiply the headcount by the per-person salary.

hints.text: You already found the Sales headcount in an earlier question.

commonMistakes: Using the wrong headcount for Sales.

questions.question: What is the monthly salary bill for the Marketing department (in ₹ lakh)?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.explanation: Marketing has 60 employees at ₹35,000 each: 60 × 35,000 = ₹21,00,000 = ₹21 lakh.
questions.method: Multiply the Marketing headcount by its per-person salary.

hints.text: Use the Marketing headcount, not the Sales one.

commonMistakes: Using the Sales salary rate instead of the Marketing rate.

questions.question: What is the total monthly salary bill for the entire company (in ₹ lakh)?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.explanation: Sales = 36 lakh, Marketing = 21 lakh, Operations + Finance (given) = 24 lakh. Total = 36 + 21 + 24 = 81 lakh.
questions.method: Add every department's bill, using the given combined figure for Operations and Finance.

hints.text: You do not need to split Operations and Finance separately for this question.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to include one of the three salary components.

questions.question: What percentage of the total workforce works in Finance?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.method: Find the Finance headcount first, then express it as a percentage of the total.

hints.text: Finance and Operations are equal, both found from the remaining employees.

commonMistakes: Using the wrong denominator, such as the remaining 120 instead of the full 300.

questions.question: If the ₹24 lakh combined salary bill for Operations and Finance is split between them in the ratio 5:7 respectively, what is Finance's salary bill (in ₹ lakh)?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.explanation: The ratio parts total 5+7=12. Finance's share = 7/12 × 24 = 14 lakh.
questions.method: Split the given combined total using the ratio's fraction for Finance.

hints.text: Finance is the second number in the ratio, so use 7 out of the 12 total parts.

commonMistakes: Using Operations' fraction (5/12) instead of Finance's (7/12).

questions.question: If the number of Sales employees increased by 25% while their salary per head stayed the same, what would be the new Sales salary bill (in ₹ lakh)?
questions.context: A company has 300 employees in total. 40% of them work in Sales. The number of employees in Marketing is half the number in Sales. The remaining employees are split equally between Operations and Finance. Each Sales employee earns ₹30,000 a month and each Marketing employee earns ₹35,000 a month. The combined monthly salary bill for Operations and Finance together is ₹24 lakh.
questions.explanation: New Sales headcount = 120 × 1.25 = 150. New bill = 150 × 30,000 = ₹45,00,000 = ₹45 lakh.
questions.method: Scale the headcount first, then recompute the salary bill.

hints.text: The per-person salary does not change, only the headcount.

commonMistakes: Increasing the salary bill by 25% of the wrong base figure.

questions.question: How many children's books did the shop sell in January?
questions.context: A bookshop sells three kinds of books: fiction, non-fiction and children's books. In January it sold 1,200 books, 45% of which were fiction. Its non-fiction sales were two-thirds of its fiction sales, and the rest were children's books. In February, the shop's total sales rose by 20% over January. Fiction sales rose by 10% and non-fiction sales by 25%, and the rest of February's sales were children's books.
questions.explanation: Fiction = 45% of 1,200 = 540. Non-fiction = two-thirds of 540 = 360. Children's books = 1,200 − 540 − 360 = 300.
questions.method: Find the two stated groups first; the children's books are the remainder.

hints.text: Find fiction and non-fiction first; children's books are the rest.

commonMistakes: Taking non-fiction as two-thirds of the whole 1,200 rather than of fiction.

questions.question: By what percentage did the shop's sales of children's books rise from January to February?
questions.context: A bookshop sells three kinds of books: fiction, non-fiction and children's books. In January it sold 1,200 books, 45% of which were fiction. Its non-fiction sales were two-thirds of its fiction sales, and the rest were children's books. In February, the shop's total sales rose by 20% over January. Fiction sales rose by 10% and non-fiction sales by 25%, and the rest of February's sales were children's books.
questions.explanation: January: fiction 540, non-fiction 360, children's 300. February: total = 1,200 × 1.2 = 1,440; fiction = 540 × 1.1 = 594; non-fiction = 360 × 1.25 = 450; children's = 1,440 − 594 − 450 = 396. Rise = (396 − 300) ÷ 300 × 100 = 32%.
questions.method: Work out February's children's books as the remainder, then compare with January.

hints.text: February's children's sales are not given — find them as the rest of February's total.

commonMistakes: Assuming children's books also rose by 20%, like the total.

questions.question: In February, fiction made up approximately what percentage of all the books the shop sold?
questions.context: A bookshop sells three kinds of books: fiction, non-fiction and children's books. In January it sold 1,200 books, 45% of which were fiction. Its non-fiction sales were two-thirds of its fiction sales, and the rest were children's books. In February, the shop's total sales rose by 20% over January. Fiction sales rose by 10% and non-fiction sales by 25%, and the rest of February's sales were children's books.
questions.explanation: February fiction = 540 × 1.1 = 594; February total = 1,200 × 1.2 = 1,440. 594 ÷ 1,440 × 100 ≈ 41.3%, so the nearest option is 41%. Fiction grew more slowly than the total, so its share fell from January's 45%.
questions.method: Update both the fiction figure and the total to February's values, then divide.

hints.text: Both the fiction figure and the total changed in February.

questions.question: Taking January and February together, what is the ratio of fiction books sold to non-fiction books sold?
questions.context: A bookshop sells three kinds of books: fiction, non-fiction and children's books. In January it sold 1,200 books, 45% of which were fiction. Its non-fiction sales were two-thirds of its fiction sales, and the rest were children's books. In February, the shop's total sales rose by 20% over January. Fiction sales rose by 10% and non-fiction sales by 25%, and the rest of February's sales were children's books.
questions.explanation: Fiction: 540 + 594 = 1,134. Non-fiction: 360 + 450 = 810. 1,134 : 810 — dividing both by 162 gives 7 : 5.
questions.method: Add each kind's two monthly figures, then simplify the ratio.

hints.text: Add each kind's January and February sales before forming the ratio.

commonMistakes: Writing the ratio the wrong way round (5 : 7).
